title: Inmates allegedly ran a $1 million scam after phones were delivered into their prisons by drone | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

Using drone-delivered phones inside their prison cells, two Georgia prisoners allegedly helped scam over 100 people out of nearly $1 million, according to a federal indictment unsealed this week.

They used the contraband phones to call and threaten people, telling them they had missed jury duty and needed to pay a fine or be arrested.

An indictment against the two men, who are still in prison, and a third defendant was unsealed on Monday and includes charges of wire fraud and money laundering. CNN is attempting to contact the defendants’ attorneys. No plea has been entered in the case, according to online records.

According to the department, prisoners in Georgia have run such jury-duty scams for over a decade.

“These defendants, who were already in prison or on parole for serious criminal offenses, did not need a weapon to target their victims,” US Attorney for the Northern District of Texas Ryan Raybould said Tuesday at a Justice Department press conference. “Instead, they weaponized fear, technology, and the public’s trust in our law enforcement and our institutions to harm victims.”

According to the indictment, the defendants, in coordination with others, would use cellphones flown in by drones as well as fake documents including arrest warrants, fake email addresses posing as US courts, and scripts designed to persuade to victims to pay the made-up fine through crypto kiosks.

The men allegedly also used services that changed their caller ID to display the phone number of a local sheriff or law enforcement agency when calling a potential victim, the indictment says.

Court documents related to the case include photos of a drone carrying contraband into a Georgia prison, an inmate posing with phones allegedly used in the scam plot, fake government websites, and a handwritten note of the scripts they allegedly read to potential victims.

The defendants allegedly built out a library of fake documents including arrest warrants they would alter with the name of the individual victims they were targeting, according to the indictment. The men, with other unnamed people, would create scripts on how to sound like a law enforcement official when calling potential victims.  In total, the Justice Department said a total of 14 people have been charged in connection with the alleged fraud scheme, and another 17 have been charged with allegedly smuggling the mobile phones into Georgia prisons.

When they had convinced someone to pay the made-up fine, the indictment alleges, the defendants would direct their victims to withdraw the money and travel to a cryptocurrency kiosk where they would transfer the money to the prisoners’ crypto exchange accounts.

Raybould warned the “case demonstrates why contraband cell phones in prisons are not merely a correctional issue; it’s a public safety issue.”

“In my humble belief, cell phones are the most dangerous thing inside a prison cell,” he added. “You can run a criminal enterprise. You can deal drugs. You can shot call. You can extort victims. And you can defraud elderly folks. All because of a cell phone allowed in a prison.”
